passages.title: From Adam to Israel and Edom
passages.summary: The family lists begin with Adam, Noah, and Abraham. They include Israel’s ancestors, neighboring peoples, and Edom’s rulers.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: Why might the book begin with Adam instead of David?

contextNote.title: Names place a small community in a larger past
contextNote.text: The book begins with Adam rather than David. Its lists connect households across many generations and peoples. Names establish relationships before the account reaches royal deeds. Read the lists as the book’s structure, not an obstacle before the story. The community’s identity reaches farther back than its kings.

passages.title: Judah’s families and David’s ancestors
passages.summary: Judah’s family list leads toward David. It also includes Tamar, workers, and descendants of an Egyptian servant.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: Which women and people from other lands appear in Judah’s family?

contextNote.title: The family record includes work as well as descent
contextNote.text: The list includes families of scribes alongside remembered ancestors. These details place skills within the community’s remembered identity. David’s ancestry appears inside a broader account of households and their contributions.

passages.title: David’s children and the royal line after exile
passages.summary: The list names David’s children and Judah’s kings. It follows Jeconiah’s descendants after exile.

passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: What hope might a surviving royal family give people after exile?

contextNote.title: The royal family line continues after royal defeat
contextNote.text: The names proceed beyond the kings into descendants after captivity. A family can continue when its throne does not. The list preserves continuity without claiming that political rule has returned.

passages.title: Judah, Jabez, craftspeople, and Simeon’s settlements

lds.text: What does Jabez ask God to protect him from?

contextNote.title: Named occupations connect ancestry with ordinary provision
contextNote.text: The record identifies craftsmen, linen workers, and potters serving the king. Family memory includes the labor that supports public life. The prayer of Jabez stands within this larger web of households.

passages.title: Eastern tribes, prayer, and captivity

contextNote.title: Birth order does not explain every inherited role

lds.text: How do the singers’ duties differ from the priests’ duties?

contextNote.title: Shared ancestry contains different forms of sacred work
contextNote.text: The chapter distinguishes priestly offerings from other Levites' tasks. Singers and settlement lists also receive extended attention. Worship rests on many households rather than one undivided office.

passages.title: Northern families, grief, and Sheerah’s building

lds.text: Which work by women does this family list remember?

contextNote.title: A woman's building work receives a place in family memory
contextNote.text: Sheerah's town building appears inside Ephraim's family account. The surrounding passage also remembers deaths and mourning. Descent lists preserve selected actions and losses rather than names alone.

passages.title: Benjamin’s families and Saul’s descendants

lds.text: How does Saul’s family list prepare for the next part of the book?

contextNote.title: The later defeated king still belongs within the recorded family
contextNote.text: Saul's descendants receive space before the account of his death. The family list preserves relatives beyond his personal reign. Royal failure does not remove the household from the community's remembered relationships.

passages.title: Jerusalem’s residents and sanctuary workers

lds.text: What daily tasks keep the temple’s worship working?

contextNote.title: Sanctuary access requires work that often remains unseen
contextNote.text: Gatekeepers guard rooms, supplies, and the opening of the house. Other workers prepare food and music. The chapter makes these repeated duties part of the community's identity after captivity.

passages.title: Saul dies at Gilboa
passages.summary: The Philistines defeat Saul and his sons. The people of Jabesh Gilead recover their bodies. The book connects Saul’s death with unfaithfulness.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain

lds.text: The Seminary manual uses Saul’s final notice to discuss trust and obedience.

contextNote.title: The account explains defeat through Saul’s conduct
contextNote.text: The closing verses explain Saul's death through unfaithfulness and failed seeking. That explanation differs from merely describing battlefield events. It also prepares the transfer of rule to David.

passages.title: David becomes king and his warriors are remembered
passages.summary: Israel’s elders anoint David at Hebron. He takes Jerusalem, and a list of warriors preserves accounts of courage and costly loyalty.

lds.text: Why does David refuse water that his men risk their lives to bring?

contextNote.title: A warrior's gift exposes the cost of royal wishes
contextNote.text: David refuses water obtained through his men's dangerous journey. He treats their risk as too costly for ordinary drinking. The named warriors' account measures loyalty through actions that endanger bodies.

passages.title: Supporters gather to David
passages.summary: Supporters join David during his flight from Saul. Amasai promises loyalty. Groups gather at Hebron with food and soldiers.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain

lds.text: How do David’s supporters help beyond bringing weapons?

contextNote.title: A gathered army also needs gathered food
contextNote.text: The assembly's joy includes supplies brought by nearby tribes. Bread and other provisions support the public transfer of kingship. Political agreement becomes visible through hospitality as well as soldiers.

passages.title: The first ark journey ends in fear
passages.summary: David gathers Israel to move the ark from Kiriath Jearim. Uzza touches it and dies. The ark remains at Obed Edom’s house.

passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: Why does David stop moving the ark? What changes when he tries again?

contextNote.title: A failed journey interrupts confidence in royal planning
contextNote.text: David consults leaders and gathers a large assembly before moving the ark. Uzza's death nevertheless stops the project. The next attempt will require more than repeating the king's original plan.

passages.title: David’s house and victories against the Philistines
passages.summary: Hiram supplies a house for David. Royal children are listed, and two Philistine attacks lead David to seek guidance.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: Why does David ask for guidance before each battle?

contextNote.title: A repeated threat receives a different instruction
contextNote.text: David asks again when the Philistines return. The answer changes his route rather than repeating the previous attack. The account distinguishes ongoing guidance from confidence based only on an earlier success.

passages.title: Levites carry the ark with music
passages.summary: David prepares a tent and appoints priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers. They carry the ark to Jerusalem. Michal watches from a window.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: What changes when David tries again to move the ark?

contextNote.title: A failed procession changes the next one
contextNote.text: David connects the earlier death with failure to follow the proper order. The second attempt gives named workers clear tasks. Music, carrying, clothing, and offerings work together. The account treats worship as shared and ordered labor. Good intention alone did not make the first attempt safe.

passages.title: Thanksgiving and two centers of worship
passages.summary: David distributes food and appoints worship workers. A thanksgiving song recalls covenant promises. Worship continues before the ark and at Gibeon.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: The Seminary manual connects this song with continuing gratitude and praise.

contextNote.title: A public celebration becomes continuing assigned work
contextNote.text: The song and food gifts do not complete the account's worship arrangements. Named workers remain before the ark and at Gibeon. Lasting practice requires daily service after the gathering ends.

passages.title: Nathan announces a house for David
passages.summary: David proposes a building for the ark. Nathan’s initial approval changes after revelation. God promises David a continuing house, and David prays.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: How does God’s promise change David’s plan for a temple?

contextNote.title: The proposed gift changes direction
contextNote.text: David intends to build a house for God. The answer instead promises a house, meaning a royal family, for David. The repeated word connects a building project with a larger claim about continuing kingship.

passages.title: Victories, tribute, dedicated treasure, and officials
passages.summary: David subdues opponents, receives gifts from Tou through Hadoram, dedicates treasure, and appoints officials.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: Where does David place the treasure gained from war?

contextNote.title: Military gain is assigned a sacred destination
contextNote.text: David dedicates collected wealth rather than treating it only as royal property. Chapter 22 later describes materials prepared for the temple. The account connects conquest with worship without hiding where the resources came from.

passages.title: Humiliated envoys and war with Ammon
passages.summary: Hanun humiliates David’s envoys. Ammon hires allies, Joab and Abishai cooperate in battle, and David defeats further Syrian forces.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain

lds.text: Come, Follow Me specifically compares this story with 2 Samuel 10–12.

contextNote.title: Advisers turn sympathy into suspected surveillance
contextNote.text: Hanun receives a warning that David's envoys intend harm. Acting on that warning converts condolence into humiliation and war. The account makes interpretation of motives politically consequential.

passages.title: Rabbah falls and Philistine warriors die
passages.summary: Joab takes Rabbah while David stays in Jerusalem. The account reports treatment of captives and later battles against Philistine warriors.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me notes that Chronicles omits negative stories about David.

contextNote.title: Selection changes what a familiar period emphasizes
contextNote.text: The opening places David in Jerusalem while Joab besieges Rabbah. Second Samuel 11 uses that setting for the Bathsheba account. Chronicles proceeds with conquest, giving this part of David's reign a different focus.

passages.title: Census, plague, and Ornan’s threshing floor
passages.summary: David orders a census despite Joab’s objection. Gad offers choices of punishment. David purchases Ornan’s site and builds an altar.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain

lds.text: David asks why the people must suffer. What does his response show about responsibility?

contextNote.title: The king names the difference between command and cost
contextNote.text: David acknowledges the census as his action while the people suffer. His plea separates his responsibility from their exposure. The altar purchase follows that recognition rather than removing the earlier deaths.

passages.title: David prepares for Solomon’s temple
passages.summary: David gathers workers and materials for the temple. Solomon will build it because David has shed blood. David calls the leaders to help.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: How does David help a task that someone else will finish?

contextNote.title: The future builder inherits resources and a restriction
contextNote.text: David gathers materials but names his bloodshed as barring him from building. Solomon receives both preparation and the assigned task. The account distinguishes supplying a project from being permitted to complete it.

passages.title: Levitical service is organized
passages.summary: David names Solomon king, counts Levites, and assigns duties. Aaron’s descendants and Moses’ descendants receive different roles.

lds.text: Which temple duties involve ordinary food, measures, and supplies?

contextNote.title: A settled sanctuary changes the form of service
contextNote.text: The Levites no longer need to carry the tent and its vessels. Their duties shift toward a permanent place of worship. Continuity of sacred service therefore includes changes in practical work.

passages.title: Priestly divisions are assigned by lot
passages.summary: David, Zadok, and Ahimelech organize priestly service. Shemaiah records the assignments, and other Levitical families also draw lots.

lds.text: How does drawing lots share duties among priestly families?

contextNote.title: Assignment by lot crosses differences in household status
contextNote.text: The closing notice names both chief fathers and younger brothers in the drawing. The procedure limits assignment by one leader's personal preference. Recorded divisions organize recurring service beyond a single occasion.

passages.title: Musicians, prophecy, and shared assignments
passages.summary: Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun lead musical families. Trained singers receive duties by lot, including teachers and students.

lds.text: Why does the music list include both teachers and students?

contextNote.title: Skill and learning belong within the same service system
contextNote.text: The lots include small and great, teacher and student. Training does not disappear when assignments use lots. The chapter places musical service within families, instruction, and ordered participation.

passages.title: Gatekeepers, stored gifts, and public duties

passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: What does faithful care of temple supplies require?

contextNote.title: Stored gifts require named responsibility
contextNote.text: Treasurers oversee dedicated goods while other Levites serve as officers and judges. These roles extend beyond performing visible worship. The account gives custody and public management a place beside sacred service.

passages.title: Army rotations and royal property
passages.summary: The list names army groups, tribal leaders, farm workers, and advisers. It also recalls the unfinished count.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: Which workers support the kingdom through farming and storage?

contextNote.title: Royal strength depends on organized turns of service
contextNote.text: Monthly army groups share duty through a rotating system. The following property workers manage food, animals, and stores. The lists describe the continuing labor beneath the king's public position.

passages.title: David gives Solomon plans and a charge
passages.summary: David gives Solomon temple plans and materials. He calls the leaders to help. He urges Solomon to seek God and begin the work.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · genealogical and historical dates uncertain
passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

lds.text: The Seminary manual emphasizes seeking God and courage in service.

contextNote.title: Receiving plans still leaves the next ruler work to do
contextNote.text: David supplies instructions and materials but urges Solomon to act. The prepared project also needs the leaders' help. Succession transfers a duty, not only possessions and status.

passages.title: Gifts, prayer, a new king, and David's death
passages.summary: David and the leaders give for the temple. David thanks God, and Solomon becomes king. The book closes with David’s death.

passages.uncertainty: Selected named towns and broad reference regions. Genealogies do not establish journeys between every marker.

contextNote.title: Royal giving rests on a prior gift
contextNote.text: David says that what the people give already came from God. The claim limits the king’s right to boast over his wealth. Leaders and people supply materials for work David will not complete. The closing scene joins giving with the transfer of rule. The temple’s future extends beyond one ruler’s life.

events.detail: The closing verses explain Saul's death through unfaithfulness and failed seeking. That explanation differs from merely describing battlefield events. It also prepares the transfer of rule to David.

guides.title: 1 Chronicles: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Names place a small community in a larger past
steps.text: The book begins with Adam rather than David. Its lists connect households across many generations and peoples. Names establish relationships before the account reaches royal deeds. Read the lists as the book’s structure, not an obstacle before the story. The community’s identity reaches farther back than its kings.

steps.title: A failed procession changes the next one
steps.text: David connects the earlier death with failure to follow the proper order. The second attempt gives named workers clear tasks. Music, carrying, clothing, and offerings work together. The account treats worship as shared and ordered labor. Good intention alone did not make the first attempt safe.

steps.title: Royal giving rests on a prior gift
steps.text: David says that what the people give already came from God. The claim limits the king’s right to boast over his wealth. Leaders and people supply materials for work David will not complete. The closing scene joins giving with the transfer of rule. The temple’s future extends beyond one ruler’s life.
